title: Theorem A
body_md:
Let $d\ge2$ and assume \eqref{eq:Goh_intro} and \eqref{eq:strongLeg_intro}. Then $u$
	admits a continuous representative, and this representative is smooth on $[0,1]$.
	Moreover, for every $t\in[0,1]$ the control value $u(t)$ is the unique unit vector
	$w$ in the kernel of the differentiated Goh operator $B(z(t))$ of
	\eqref{eq:Bmap} such that $T_{z(t)}(w,y,y)>0$ for every non-zero $y\perp w$ (see
	\eqref{eq:trilinear}), and it depends smoothly on the state-costate pair
	$z(t)=(q(t),\lambda(t))$.
head: environment

title: Theorem B
body_md:
Under the same hypotheses there exist $t_*\in(0,1]$ and constants $\eta>0$,
	$C_4>0$, all independent of $t$, such that for every $t\in(0,t_*]$ and every
	variation $\mathbf v\in L^2([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d)$ satisfying the admissibility constraint
	\eqref{eq:conepointwise},
	\[
		\left\langle\ell_t,G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right\rangle
		\ \ge\ \eta\left\|\mathbf V\right\|_{\mathcal H}^2
		-C_4\left|G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right|^2 ,
	\]
	where $G^t_{q(t)}$ is the end-point map read in the adapted chart of
	Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}, $\ell_t$ is the abnormal covector in that chart,
	$\mathbf V$ is the primitive of $\mathbf v$, and $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal H}$ is the norm
	\eqref{eq:Hnorm}.
head: environment

title: Theorem C
body_md:
Under the same hypotheses there exists $t_*\in(0,1]$ such that, for every
	$t\in(0,t_*]$, the arc $\gamma_u|_{[0,t]}$ is rigid and minimizes the length among all
	admissible curves joining $q$ to $q(t)$: if $\gamma_{\tilde u}$ is an admissible curve
	joining $q$ to $q(t)$ with $\ell(\gamma_{\tilde u})\le t$, then $\ell(\gamma_{\tilde u})=t$
	and $\gamma_{\tilde u}$ coincides with $\gamma_u|_{[0,t]}$ up to reparametrization. In
	particular, $u|_{[0,t]}$ is the unique length-minimizing control of constant speed
	joining $q$ to $q(t)$.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:notdiscarded}
	In Section~\ref{sec:separation} we shall need the expansion of the end-point map for
	arbitrary admissible variations, not only for those in the kernel of
	$d_0G^t_{q(t)}$. The second summand of \eqref{eq:Second_order_differential} does not

	defect $\left|d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right|$, which by Lemma~\ref{lem:defect} is

	naive scheme of Subsection~\ref{ssec:onedir} would fail.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\xi_{\min}(t):=\min_{w\in u(t)^\perp,|w|=1}Q^{t}(w)$. Since $Q^t$ is homogeneous
	of degree $2$, we have $Q^t\ge0$ on $u(t)^\perp$ if and only if $\xi_{\min}(t)\ge0$. In
	particular $\xi_{\min}(t)\ge0$ for almost every $t\in[0,1]$, that is
	$\mu\left(\{t\in[0,1]\mid\xi_{\min}(t)<0\}\right)=0$; hence $0$ is an essential lower
	bound for $\xi_{\min}$ and, by definition of essential infimum as the supremum of such
	bounds, $\mathrm{ess\,inf}_{t\in[0,1]}\xi_{\min}(t)\ge0$.

label: rmk:strongLeg
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:strongLeg}
	Condition \eqref{eq:strongLeg} is commonly referred to as the strong generalized
	Legendre condition. In \cite{AS95,AS96} the inequality is assumed to hold at
	all points $t\in[0,1]$, an assumption which considerably simplifies the proof of
	the smoothness of $u$. Throughout this paper we assume its validity only on the set of
	Lebesgue points of $u$, and we recover the smoothness by a compactness argument along
	the essential graph \eqref{eq:essgraph}. For rank-two distributions,
	\eqref{eq:strongLeg} has been used to prove the local $W^{1,1}$-minimality of nice
	abnormal curves, i.e.\ under \eqref{eq:nice}; see Subsection~\ref{ssec:nice} and
	Remark~\ref{rmk:niceanalogy}.

label: lem:rank
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:rank}
	Let $z=(q,\lambda)\in T^*M$, let $w_0\in\ker B(z)$ with $|w_0|=1$, and assume that
	there exists $c>0$ such that
	\[
		T_z(w_0,y,y)\ge c|y|^2\qquad\text{for every }y\in w_0^\perp .
	\]
	Then $\ker B(z)=\mathrm{span}\{w_0\}$. Moreover $R(q,\lambda,w_0)$ is symmetric and
	$\ker R(q,\lambda,w_0)=\mathrm{span}\{w_0\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $w\in\ker B(z)$ with $w\perp w_0$ and $|w|=1$. Since $w\in\ker B(z)$, the bilinear
	form $T_z(w,\cdot,\cdot)$ is symmetric in its last two arguments, whence
	$T_z(w,w_0,w)=T_z(w,w,w_0)=0$, the last equality following from \eqref{eq:T1}. On the
	other hand, again by \eqref{eq:T1}, $T_z(w,w_0,w)=-T_z(w_0,w,w)$. Combining the two
	identities we obtain $T_z(w_0,w,w)=0$, contradicting $T_z(w_0,w,w)\ge c|w|^2=c>0$.
	Therefore $\ker B(z)\cap w_0^\perp=\{0\}$, and since $w_0\in\ker B(z)$ the first claim
	follows.

	As for the second claim, $w_0\in\ker B(z)$ means that $R(q,\lambda,w_0)$ is symmetric,
	and then \eqref{eq:T2} gives $R(q,\lambda,w_0)w_0=R(q,\lambda,w_0)^Tw_0=0$, so that
	$\ker R(q,\lambda,w_0)\supseteq\mathrm{span}\{w_0\}$. Conversely, any
	$y\in\ker R(q,\lambda,w_0)\cap w_0^\perp$ satisfies
	$0=\langle y,R(q,\lambda,w_0)y\rangle=T_z(w_0,y,y)\ge c|y|^2$, hence $y=0$.
head: environment

label: rmk:geomrank
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:geomrank}
	The operator $B(z)$ measures the failure of $\lambda$ to annihilate the brackets of
	length three of the form $[X_a,[X_b,X_c]]$; the differentiated Goh condition says that
	the control direction lies in its kernel. Lemma~\ref{lem:rank} states that coercivity
	of the Legendre form forces that kernel to be as small as it can possibly be, namely a
	line. Since the line is spanned by $u(t)$, the control direction is determined -- up to a sign, fixed in Lemma~\ref{lem:sign} by the positivity of $T_z$ -- by the
	state-costate pair alone: the extremal is, in this sense, a genuine characteristic
	curve of a smooth field of directions, which is the true reason behind its smoothness.
head: environment

label: lem:sign
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sign}
	Let $d\ge2$, let $z=(q,\lambda)\in T^*M$ and let $w_0\in S^{d-1}$ satisfy the
	hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:rank}. Then $w_0$ is the unique $w\in S^{d-1}$ such that
	\[
		B(z)w=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_z(w,y,y)>0\quad\text{for every }0\neq y\in w^\perp .
	\]
	Moreover the bordered matrix
	\[
		\begin{pmatrix}R(q,\lambda,w_0)&w_0\\ w_0^T&0\end{pmatrix}
	\]
	is invertible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:rank}, any $w$ as in the statement belongs to
	$\mathrm{span}\{w_0\}\cap S^{d-1}=\{\pm w_0\}$. Since $T_z$ is linear in its first argument,
	$T_z(-w_0,y,y)=-T_z(w_0,y,y)\le-c|y|^2$ for $y\in w_0^\perp=(-w_0)^\perp$, so that
	$-w_0$ violates the positivity requirement, the space $w_0^\perp$ being non-trivial
	because $d\ge2$. Hence $w=w_0$.

	For the invertibility assertion, assume that
	\[
		\begin{pmatrix}R(q,\lambda,w_0)&w_0\\ w_0^T&0\end{pmatrix}
		\begin{pmatrix}y\\ \alpha\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}.
	\]
	The second equation gives $y\in w_0^\perp$. Multiplying the first equation
	$R(q,\lambda,w_0)y+\alpha w_0=0$ by $w_0^T$, and using that $R(q,\lambda,w_0)$ is
	symmetric with $R(q,\lambda,w_0)w_0=0$, so that
	$w_0^TR(q,\lambda,w_0)y=\left\langle R(q,\lambda,w_0)w_0,y\right\rangle=0$, we deduce
	$\alpha|w_0|^2=0$, i.e.\ $\alpha=0$. This leaves $R(q,\lambda,w_0)y=0$ with
	$y\in w_0^\perp$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:rank} forces $y=0$.
head: environment

label: lem:essential-graph
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:essential-graph}
	The set $\mathcal G$ is compact, and every $(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*)\in\mathcal G$ satisfies
	\[
		|w_*|=1,\qquad B(q_*,\lambda_*)w_*=0,\qquad R(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*)w_*=0 .
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The curve $t\mapsto(q(t),\lambda(t))$ is continuous, hence its image
	$\Gamma:=\{(q(t),\lambda(t)):t\in[0,1]\}$ is compact. Since $|u(t)|=1$ for $t\in E$, we
	have $\mathcal G_0\subseteq\Gamma\times S^{d-1}$, and therefore $\mathcal G$ is compact,
	being a closed subset of a compact set.

	For every $t\in E$ the differentiated Goh condition gives $B(z(t))u(t)=0$ and hence, by
	\eqref{eq:T2} and the symmetry of $R(q(t),\lambda(t),u(t))$, also
	$R(q(t),\lambda(t),u(t))u(t)=0$. The maps $z\mapsto B(z)$ and $(z,w)\mapsto R(z,w)w$
	are smooth, hence continuous, so that the sets $\{(z,w):B(z)w=0\}$,
	$\{(z,w):R(z,w)w=0\}$ and $T^*M\times S^{d-1}$ are closed. Since $\mathcal G_0$ is
	contained in all of them, so is its closure $\mathcal G$.
head: environment

label: lem:uniform-bordered-invertibility
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:uniform-bordered-invertibility}
	For every $(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*)\in\mathcal G$ one has
	\[
		\left\langle y,R(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*)y\right\rangle\ge c|y|^2
		\qquad\text{for every }y\in w_*^\perp .
	\]
	Consequently $\ker B(q_*,\lambda_*)=\mathrm{span}\{w_*\}$, the bordered matrix
	\[
		\mathcal M(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*):=
		\begin{pmatrix}R(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*)&w_*\\ w_*^T&0\end{pmatrix}
	\]
	is invertible, and
	$\sup_{\zeta\in\mathcal G}\left\|\mathcal M(\zeta)^{-1}\right\|<\infty$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(q(t_n),\lambda(t_n),u(t_n))\to(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*)$ with $t_n\in E$. Fix
	$y\in w_*^\perp$ and set $y_n:=y-\left\langle y,u(t_n)\right\rangle u(t_n)\in
	u(t_n)^\perp$. Since $u(t_n)\to w_*$ and $\langle y,w_*\rangle=0$, we have $y_n\to y$.
	The strong Legendre condition, written through \eqref{eq:RviaT}, gives
	$\left\langle y_n,R(q(t_n),\lambda(t_n),u(t_n))y_n\right\rangle\ge c|y_n|^2$, and
	passing to the limit, by continuity of $R$,
	$\left\langle y,R(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*)y\right\rangle\ge c|y|^2$.

	By Lemma~\ref{lem:essential-graph} we have $B(q_*,\lambda_*)w_*=0$, so that
	Lemma~\ref{lem:rank} applies at $(q_*,\lambda_*)$ with $w_0=w_*$ and yields
	$\ker B(q_*,\lambda_*)=\mathrm{span}\{w_*\}$ together with
	$\ker R(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*)=\mathrm{span}\{w_*\}$; Lemma~\ref{lem:sign} then gives the
	invertibility of $\mathcal M(q_*,\lambda_*,w_*)$. Finally, $\zeta\mapsto\mathcal
	M(\zeta)$ is continuous on the compact set $\mathcal G$ and invertible at each of its
	points, hence $\zeta\mapsto\mathcal M(\zeta)^{-1}$ is continuous on $\mathcal G$ and its
	norm attains a finite maximum there.
head: environment

label: prop:ucont
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:ucont}
	Assume that the Goh condition \eqref{eq:Goh_section} and the strong Legendre condition
	\eqref{eq:strongLeg} hold, and let $d\ge2$. Then, for every $t_*\in[0,1]$, there exists
	a unique $w_*\in S^{d-1}$ such that $(q(t_*),\lambda(t_*),w_*)\in\mathcal G$.
	Consequently, $u|_E$ admits a unique continuous extension $\bar u:[0,1]\to S^{d-1}$.
head: environment

label: eq:linearGoh
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $t\in E$. Applying \eqref{eq:derpairing} with $Y=[X_i,X_j]$ to the identity
	$\langle\lambda(s),[X_i,X_j](q(s))\rangle=0$, valid for every $s$ by
	\eqref{eq:Goh_section}, we obtain
	$\langle\lambda(t),[X_{u(t)},[X_i,X_j]](q(t))\rangle=0$ for all $i,j$, which by
	\eqref{eq:Bmap} and \eqref{eq:Gohviatrilinear} reads
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:linearGoh}
		B(z(t))u(t)=0 .
	\end{equation}
	Together with \eqref{eq:strongLeg} and \eqref{eq:RviaT}, Lemma~\ref{lem:rank} yields
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:kernelline}
		\ker B(z(t))=\ker R(q(t),\lambda(t),u(t))=\mathrm{span}\{u(t)\},\qquad t\in E.
	\end{equation}
	Fix $t_*$. Since $E$ is dense, choose $t_n\in E$ with $t_n\to t_*$. Up to a
	subsequence, $u(t_n)\to w_*\in S^{d-1}$, and continuity of $z$ gives
	$(z(t_*),w_*)\in\mathcal G$.

	Let $w_*,\widetilde w_*\in S^{d-1}$ be such that $(z(t_*),w_*)$ and
	$(z(t_*),\widetilde w_*)$ belong to $\mathcal G$, and choose sequences
	$\tau_n,\sigma_n\in E$ with $(z(\tau_n),u(\tau_n))\to(z(t_*),w_*)$ and
	$(z(\sigma_n),u(\sigma_n))\to(z(t_*),\widetilde w_*)$. Passing to the limit in
	\eqref{eq:linearGoh} gives $B(z(t_*))w_*=B(z(t_*))\widetilde w_*=0$. For
	$y\in w_*^\perp$, set $y_n=y-\langle y,u(\tau_n)\rangle u(\tau_n)$; then $y_n\to y$ and the
	strong Legendre inequality passes to the limit:
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:limitLegendre}
		T_{z(t_*)}(w_*,y,y)\ge c|y|^2,\qquad y\in w_*^\perp .
	\end{equation}
	Lemma~\ref{lem:rank} gives $\ker B(z(t_*))=\mathrm{span}\{w_*\}$, hence
	$\widetilde w_*=\pm w_*$. The same limiting inequality for $\widetilde w_*$ excludes
	the negative sign, because $d\ge2$ and $T_z(-w_*,y,y)=-T_z(w_*,y,y)<0$ for non-zero
	$y\in w_*^\perp$. Thus every fiber is a singleton.

	Define $\bar u(t)$ as its unique element; if $t\in E$, then $\bar u(t)=u(t)$. If
	$t_n\to t_*$ and a subsequence $\bar u(t_{n_k})\to w$, closedness of $\mathcal G$
	implies $(z(t_*),w)\in\mathcal G$, hence $w=\bar u(t_*)$. Compactness of the sphere then
	implies convergence of the whole sequence, so $\bar u$ is continuous.

label: lem:quantitative-IFT
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:quantitative-IFT}
	Let $P,Y,Z$ be finite dimensional normed spaces, let $\Phi:P\times Y\to Z$ be $C^2$,
	and let $K\subset P\times Y$ be compact with $\Phi\equiv0$ on $K$. Assume that
	$D_y\Phi$ is invertible at every point of $K$, with
	$\sup_K\|D_y\Phi^{-1}\|\le M$. If $D_y\Phi$ is $L$-Lipschitz and $D_p\Phi$ is bounded
	by $N$ on a compact neighborhood of $K$, then any $r,\rho>0$ satisfying
	\[
		ML(r+\rho)\le\frac12,\qquad MNr\le\frac\rho2 ,
	\]
	and remaining inside that neighborhood, have the following property: for each
	$(p_*,y_*)\in K$ and each $p\in B_r(p_*)$, the equation $\Phi(p,y)=0$ has a unique
	solution in $B_\rho(y_*)$, depending smoothly on $p$.
head: environment
name: Quantitative implicit-function lemma

label: prop:smooth
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:Psi
title: Proof
body_md:
Define
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Psi}
		\Psi(q,\lambda,w,\mu)=
		\begin{pmatrix}R(q,\lambda,w)w+\mu w\\[1mm]\frac12(|w|^2-1)\end{pmatrix}.
	\end{equation}
	Along the extremal, $\Psi(q(t),\lambda(t),u(t),0)=0$. Writing
	$F(q,\lambda,w)=R(q,\lambda,w)w$, so that $F_i(q,\lambda,w)=T_z(w,e_i,w)$, and
	differentiating in $w$ along a direction $m\in\mathbb{R}^d$ we obtain
	\[
		\big(D_wF(q,\lambda,w)m\big)_i\Big|_{w=u(t)}
		=T_{z(t)}(m,e_i,u(t))+\big(R(q(t),\lambda(t),u(t))m\big)_i .
	\]
	The first summand equals $-\left\langle\lambda(t),[X_{u(t)},[X_m,X_i]](q(t))\right\rangle$
	and vanishes by the differentiated Goh condition \eqref{eq:linearGoh}; therefore
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:jacPsi}
		D_{(w,\mu)}\Psi(q(t),\lambda(t),u(t),0)=
		\begin{pmatrix}R(q(t),\lambda(t),u(t))&u(t)\\ u(t)^T&0\end{pmatrix}
		=\mathcal M(q(t),\lambda(t),u(t)).
	\end{equation}
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-bordered-invertibility} these matrices are invertible with
	uniformly bounded inverse on the compact essential graph. Applying
	Lemma~\ref{lem:quantitative-IFT} with $p=(q,\lambda)$ and $y=(w,\mu)$ we obtain radii
	$r,\rho>0$, independent of the base point, and unique smooth local branches
	$(w_{\zeta_*},\mu_{\zeta_*})$. Taking the scalar product of the first block of
	$\Psi=0$ with $w$, and using $R(z,w)^Tw=0$ from \eqref{eq:T2} together with $|w|=1$, we
	get $\mu_{\zeta_*}=0$.

	Continuity of $(z(t),u(t))$ and local uniqueness imply, near every $t_0$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:localbranch}
		u(t)=w_{t_0}(z(t)),
	\end{equation}
	and on overlaps both branches coincide with the already fixed continuous
	representative. Since the state-costate equations
	\[
		\begin{cases}
			\dot q(s)=X_{u(s)}(q(s)),\\[1mm]
			\dot\lambda(s)=-\,\partial_q\left\langle\lambda(s),X_{u(s)}(q(s))\right\rangle ,
		\end{cases}
	\]
	i.e.\ the lift to $T^*M$ of the flow of $X_{u}$,
	have continuous right-hand side, $z=(q,\lambda)\in C^1$, and \eqref{eq:localbranch}
	gives $u\in C^1$. If $u\in C^k$, the state-costate equations give $z\in C^{k+1}$ and
	the smooth branch gives $u\in C^{k+1}$. Induction proves smoothness.

label: rmk:niceanalogy
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:niceanalogy}
	Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth} is the higher-rank counterpart of the regularity
	statements available for nice abnormal extremals of rank-two distributions
	\cite{AS95},\cite[Chapter~12]{ABB20}. As explained in Subsection~\ref{ssec:nice}, for
	$d=2$ the niceness condition \eqref{eq:nice} is equivalent to $B(z)\neq0$ and hence,
	$\Lambda^2(\mathbb{R}^2)^*$ being one-dimensional, to \eqref{eq:onedim}. For $d\ge3$ the two
	requirements part company: $B(z)\neq0$ is one scalar condition, whereas
	\eqref{eq:onedim} is the maximality $\mathrm{rank} B(z)=d-1$. What the present section shows is
	that the strong Legendre condition delivers \eqref{eq:onedim} for free, and with it the
	whole regularity theory, without any assumption on the flag $\Delta\subset\Delta^2
	\subset\Delta^3$.

name: Higher rank versus niceness

label: lem:adapted
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:adapted}
	There exist $t_0\in(0,1]$, open sets $\mathcal O_1\subset\subset\mathcal O\subset M$
	containing the arc $\Gamma_{t_0}:=q([0,t_0])$, a chart
	$\kappa:\mathcal O\to\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, and a smooth orthonormal frame
	$X_1,\dots,X_d$ of $\Delta$ on $\mathcal O$, with the following properties.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(i)] (Straightening)
		$X_1(q(s))=\dot q(s)$ and $u(s)=e_1$ for every $s\in[0,t_0]$.
		\item[(ii)] (Coframe) There are covectors
		$\eta_1(t),\dots,\eta_d(t)\in T^*_{q(t)}M$, depending continuously on
		$t\in[0,t_0]$, with
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:coframe}
			\left\langle\eta_k(t),X_j(q(t))\right\rangle=\delta_{kj},
			\qquad j,k=1,\dots,d,
			\qquad
			C_\eta:=\sup_{t\in[0,t_0]}\max_{1\le i\le d}|\eta_i(t)|<\infty .
		\end{equation}
		\item[(iii)] (Affine abnormal coordinate) Setting
		$\kappa_t:=\kappa-\kappa(q(t))$ and
		$\ell_t:=\lambda(t)\circ d_{\kappa(q(t))}\kappa^{-1}\in(\mathbb{R}^n)^*$, the function
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:alinear}
			a_t:\mathcal O\to\mathbb{R},\qquad a_t(x):=\left\langle\ell_t,\kappa_t(x)\right\rangle
		\end{equation}
		satisfies $a_t(q(t))=0$, $d_{q(t)}a_t=\lambda(t)$ and
		$D^k_y\left(a_t\circ\kappa_t^{-1}\right)\equiv0$ for every $k\ge2$; moreover
		$C_\ell:=\sup_{t\in[0,t_0]}|\ell_t|<\infty$.
		\item[(iv)] (Uniform bounds) Let $\mathcal B:=\kappa(\overline{\mathcal
		O_1})$, a compact subset of $\Omega$. Every supremum of the coordinate expressions
		of the vector fields $X_i$, of their transported versions
		$X^\tau_i:=e^{(t-\tau)X_1}_*X_i$, and of all their partial derivatives with respect
		to $x$ and $\tau$ of total order at most three, taken over $\mathcal B$ and over
		$\tau,t\in[0,t_0]$, is finite.
		\item[(v)] (Localization) Set
		\[
			L_0:=\sqrt d\,\max_{1\le i\le d}\sup_{\tau,t\in[0,t_0],\,x\in\mathcal B}
			\left|X_i^\tau(x)\right|,
			\qquad
			\delta:=\inf_{s\in[0,t_0]}\operatorname{dist}\big(\kappa(q(s)),
			\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\kappa(\mathcal O_1)\big).
		\]
		Then $\delta>0$ and $2L_0t_0<\delta$.
	\end{itemize}

name: Adapted normalization

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $|u(t)|=1$ and $X_1,\dots,X_d$ are linearly independent,
	$\dot q(t)=X_{u(t)}(q(t))\neq 0$; after decreasing $t_0>0$, the arc $q|_{[0,t_0]}$ is a
	smooth embedded curve, contained in a contractible coordinate neighborhood
	$\mathcal O$ with chart $\kappa$. Extend the coefficients of $u$ off the arc by
	$\widetilde u_i(x):=u(s)$ if $x$ lies on the slice of a tubular neighborhood through
	$q(s)$, put $\widetilde Y:=\sum_i\widetilde u_iX_i$ and, after shrinking $\mathcal O$
	so that $\widetilde Y\neq0$,
	\[
		Y_1:=\frac{\widetilde Y}{\|\widetilde Y\|_g} ,
	\]
	a smooth unit horizontal field with $Y_1(q(s))=\dot q(s)$. Completing $Y_1$ to a smooth
	orthonormal frame $Y_1,\dots,Y_d$ of $\Delta$ on the contractible set $\mathcal O$ and
	relabelling $Y_i$ as $X_i$ gives (i). Since $X_1(q(t)),\dots,X_d(q(t))$ are linearly
	independent, the covectors in (ii) exist; they are not unique when $d<n$, and we fix
	once and for all the choice obtained by Gram--Schmidt orthonormalization of
	$X_1(q(t)),\dots,X_d(q(t))$ with respect to an auxiliary Riemannian metric on $M$,
	declaring $\eta_k(t)$ to vanish on the corresponding orthogonal complement; this choice
	is continuous in $t$, whence $C_\eta<\infty$ by compactness of $[0,t_0]$. Item (iii)
	is immediate: $\kappa_t$ is a translation of $\kappa$, so $d\kappa_t=d\kappa$ and
	$a_t\circ\kappa_t^{-1}=\left\langle\ell_t,\cdot\right\rangle$ is linear; continuity of
	$t\mapsto\ell_t$ gives $C_\ell<\infty$. Finally, choose $\mathcal O_1$ with
	$\Gamma_{t_0}\subset\mathcal O_1\subset\subset\mathcal O$ and decrease $t_0$ once more
	so that all the flow segments occurring below stay in $\overline{\mathcal O_1}$; all
	the data in (iv) are smooth functions on the compact set
	$\mathcal B\times[0,t_0]\times[0,t_0]$, hence bounded there. As for (v),
	$\delta>0$ because $s\mapsto\kappa(q(s))$ is continuous on a compact interval with
	values in the open set $\kappa(\mathcal O_1)$; moreover, when $t_0$ decreases $L_0$ does
	not increase and $\delta$ does not decrease, so that $2L_0t_0<\delta$ is obtained by
	decreasing $t_0$ once more.
head: environment

label: rmk:frame
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:frame}
	The frame of Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted} differs from the one used so far by a smooth
	$O(d)$-valued function $\mathcal R$ on $\mathcal O$: a horizontal curve $\gamma$ with
	control $\tilde u$ in the old frame has control $\mathcal R(\gamma)^T\tilde u$ in the
	new one. This correspondence is a smooth change of variables between neighborhoods of
	$u$ in $L^2$ which preserves pointwise the norm of the control, hence the length, the
	energy and the end-point. Consequently the image of the differential of the end-point
	map, and the covectors orthogonal to it, do not depend on the frame. That the Goh
	condition and the Legendre form are not affected either is the content of
	Lemma~\ref{lem:frameinv} below, since the brackets of the new fields contain
	derivatives of the coefficients of $\mathcal R$.
head: environment
name: Change of frame

label: lem:frameinv
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:frameinv}
	Let $X_1,\dots,X_d$ be the frame used so far, let $Y_a=\sum_{i}\mathcal R_{ia}X_i$,
	$a=1,\dots,d$, be the frame of Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}, and let $q\in\mathcal O$,
	$\lambda\in T^*_qM$ with $\lambda\perp\Delta_q$ and $\lambda\perp\Delta^2_q$. Then,
	writing $\mathcal R=\mathcal R(q)$,
	\[
		\langle\lambda,[Y_a,Y_b](q)\rangle
		=\sum_{i,j}\mathcal R_{ia}\mathcal R_{jb}\,\langle\lambda,[X_i,X_j](q)\rangle,
	\]
	\[
		\langle\lambda,[[Y_a,Y_b],Y_c](q)\rangle
		=\sum_{i,j,k}\mathcal R_{ia}\mathcal R_{jb}\mathcal R_{kc}\,
		\langle\lambda,[[X_i,X_j],X_k](q)\rangle .
	\]
	In particular, \eqref{eq:Goh_section} and \eqref{eq:strongLeg} hold in the frame
	$Y_1,\dots,Y_d$ with the same constant $c$.
head: environment
name: Invariance under change of frame

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A,B,C$ be smooth sections of $\Delta$ and $f$ a smooth function. Then
	\[
		[fA,B]=f[A,B]-(Bf)A,\qquad
		[[A,B],fC]=f[[A,B],C]+([A,B]f)\,C,
	\]
	\[
		[[fA,B],C]=f[[A,B],C]-(Cf)[A,B]-(Bf)[A,C]+(C(Bf))\,A ,
	\]
	and the case of $fB$ follows from $[[A,fB],C]=-[[fB,A],C]$. Since $\lambda$ annihilates
	$\Delta_q$ and $[A,B](q),[A,C](q)\in\Delta^2_q$, all the correction terms vanish after
	pairing with $\lambda$. Hence $\langle\lambda,[A,B](q)\rangle$ and
	$\langle\lambda,[[A,B],C](q)\rangle$ are multilinear over $C^\infty$ functions in the
	sections of $\Delta$, i.e.\ they depend only on the values of $A,B,C$ at $q$, and the
	two formulas follow by expanding $Y_a=\sum_i\mathcal R_{ia}X_i$. By
	\eqref{eq:Goh_section} and the Pontryagin Maximum Principle the hypothesis on
	$\lambda=\lambda(t)$ holds for every $t$, so the first formula gives the Goh condition
	for the $Y$'s. Moreover $Y_1(q(t))=\dot q(t)=X_{u(t)}(q(t))$ gives
	$\mathcal R(q(t))e_1=u(t)$, so that, by the second formula and the orthogonality of
	$\mathcal R$, for $w\perp e_1$,
	$\langle\lambda(t),[[Y_1,Y_w],Y_w](q(t))\rangle
	=Q^t\big(\mathcal R(q(t))w\big)\ge c\,|\mathcal R(q(t))w|^2=c|w|^2$, because
	$\mathcal R(q(t))w\perp u(t)$.
head: environment

label: rmk:chart
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:chart}
	Three features of Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted} are used repeatedly, and it is worth
	isolating them once, so as not to return to the matter again.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(a)] The parameter $t$ only moves the origin:
		$\kappa_t=\kappa-\kappa(q(t))$. Since translations do not affect derivatives, all
		coordinate derivatives may be computed in the single fixed chart $\kappa$, and all
		the resulting bounds are uniform in $t$. In the coordinates $\kappa_t$ the set
		$\mathcal B$ is translated by $-\kappa(q(t))$ and, by Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(v), the
		open ball of radius $\delta$ centred at the origin is contained in the translated
		image of $\mathcal O_1$, hence in the translated set $\mathcal B$. From now on we identify points of
		$\mathcal O$ with their coordinates through $\kappa_t$; in particular
		$q(t)$ becomes the origin of $\mathbb{R}^n$, $G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)$ is regarded as a vector of
		$\mathbb{R}^n$, and $a_t(x)=\left\langle\ell_t,x\right\rangle$.
		\item[(b)]The abnormal coordinate $a_t$ is affine, so its derivatives of order $\ge2$ vanish identically.
		Every nonlinear term in the expansions below comes from the coordinate expressions
		of the transported fields and of their flows, never from $a_t$.
		\item[(c)] Every constant denoted by $C$, $K$, $\Lambda$, $L$ or
		$\delta$, with or without subscripts, is a supremum of the type described in
		Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(iv); it depends only on the reference extremal, on the
		adapted frame and coframe, and on $t_0$, and never on $t\in(0,t_0]$ nor on the
		variation.
	\end{itemize}
head: environment
name: How the chart is used

label: rmk:geomstraight
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:geomstraight}
No equiregularity assumption is used in this construction. The frame is adapted only to the reference direction $u$, and not to the flag $\Delta \subseteq \Delta^2 \subseteq \cdots$, while $\kappa$ is an arbitrary smooth chart, rather than a system of privileged coordinates.
	
    Item (i) of Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted} makes the reference control constant, equal
	to $e_1$. All the geometry is thereby transferred to the frame, and the Goh condition
	acquires a transparent meaning: $\lambda(t)$ annihilates $\Delta_{q(t)}$ by the PMP and
	$\Delta^2_{q(t)}$ by \eqref{eq:Goh_section}, so the abnormal codirection is invisible to
	first and second order along $\Delta$, and the leading term it sees is the
	length-three bracket $\left[[X_{e_1},X_w],X_w\right]$ --- precisely the Legendre form.
	Coercivity of $Q^t$ is thus a uniform transversality requirement of the arc with respect
	to the flag $\Delta\subset\Delta^2\subset\Delta^3$, in all the $d-1$ directions
	orthogonal to the motion.
head: environment
name: Geometry of the adapted normalization

label: lem:reparam
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:reparam}
	Let $\gamma_{\tilde u}$ be an admissible curve on $[0,t]$ with $\mathsf{L}(\tilde u)>0$, and
	set $\eta:=\gamma_{\tilde u}\circ\varphi^\#$. Then $\gamma_{\tilde u}=\eta\circ\varphi$,
	$\eta$ is an admissible curve with the same end-points as $\gamma_{\tilde u}$, and its
	control $\tilde u_\varphi$ satisfies $|\tilde u_\varphi|=\mathsf{L}(\tilde u)/t$ a.e.\ on
	$[0,t]$.
head: environment
name: Constant-speed reparametrization

title: Proof
body_md:
On every interval where $\varphi$ is constant one has $\tilde u=0$ a.e., hence
	$\gamma_{\tilde u}$ is constant there. Since $\varphi$ is constant on
	$[\varphi^\#(\varphi(\tau)),\tau]$, we get
	$\gamma_{\tilde u}(\tau)=\gamma_{\tilde u}(\varphi^\#(\varphi(\tau)))=\eta(\varphi(\tau))$,
	and evaluating at $\tau=0,t$ gives the claim on the end-points. Let $d_{SR}$ be the
	sub-Riemannian distance. For $0\le s_1\le s_2\le t$ and $a_i:=\varphi^\#(s_i)$ we have
	$a_1\le a_2$ and
	\[
		d_{SR}\big(\eta(s_1),\eta(s_2)\big)\le\ell\big(\gamma_{\tilde u}|_{[a_1,a_2]}\big)
		=\int_{a_1}^{a_2}|\tilde u|=\frac{\mathsf{L}(\tilde u)}{t}\big(\varphi(a_2)-\varphi(a_1)\big)
		=\frac{\mathsf{L}(\tilde u)}{t}(s_2-s_1).
	\]
	Thus $\eta$ is Lipschitz with respect to $d_{SR}$; hence it is admissible, and the norm
	of its control is its metric speed, so that $|\tilde u_\varphi|\le\mathsf{L}(\tilde u)/t$ a.e.\
	(see e.g.\ \cite{ABB20}). Finally, $\eta=\gamma_{\tilde u}\circ\varphi^\#$ and
	$\gamma_{\tilde u}=\eta\circ\varphi$ are compositions with monotone maps, under which the
	length can only decrease; hence $\ell(\eta)=\ell(\gamma_{\tilde u})=\mathsf{L}(\tilde u)$,
	i.e.\ $\int_0^t|\tilde u_\varphi|=\mathsf{L}(\tilde u)$. Together with
	$|\tilde u_\varphi|\le\mathsf{L}(\tilde u)/t$ on an interval of length $t$, this forces
	equality a.e.
head: environment

label: rmk:cone
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:cone}
	Constraint \eqref{eq:conepointwise} says that $u+\mathbf v$ takes values in the closed unit
	ball, i.e.\ that the competitor is no longer than the reference arc at every instant;
	geometrically, $\mathbf v(\tau)$ ranges in the closed unit ball centred at $-u$, which is
	tangent at the origin to the hyperplane $\{v_1=0\}$. Its linearization at the origin is
	the half-space \eqref{eq:cone}. The set of admissible variations is therefore convex
	and bounded in $L^\infty$, but it is neither a linear subspace nor a cone, since it is
	not invariant under multiplication by positive scalars: this is what makes all the
	estimates below uniform, rather than asymptotic as $\mathbf v\to0$.
head: environment
name: The admissible set

label: rmk:Hnorm
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:Hnorm}
	The norm \eqref{eq:Hnorm} is evaluated on the primitive $\mathbf V$ of the variation,
	not on the variation itself; it is therefore a weak, $H^{-1}$-type norm on $\mathbf v$, and
	it is exactly the norm in which the reduced Hessian \eqref{eq:hessGnoV1} is bounded.
	The boundary term $|x(t)|^2$ cannot be dispensed with: \eqref{eq:hessGnoV1} genuinely
	depends on $V(t)$, and this is the analytic trace of the fact that the end-point is
	fixed.
head: environment
name: What $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal H}$ measures

label: prop:completion
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Equip $\mathcal K$ with the product Hilbert norm
	$\|(a,f)\|_{\mathcal K}^2=|a|^2+\|f\|_{L^2}^2$. The linear map
	\[
		\Phi:H^1([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d)\longrightarrow\mathcal K,\qquad\Phi(x)=(x(t),x),
	\]
	is by construction an isometry from
	$\big(H^1([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d),\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal H}\big)$ into the complete Hilbert space
	$\mathcal K$; it therefore suffices to prove that its image is dense. Let
	$(a,f)\in\mathcal K$. Since $C_c^\infty\big((0,t),\mathbb{R}^d\big)$ is dense in
	$L^2([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d)$, choose $g_n\in C_c^\infty\big((0,t),\mathbb{R}^d\big)$ with
	$\|g_n-f\|_{L^2}\to0$; compactness of the supports guarantees $g_n(t)=0$ for every $n$.
	For $n>1/t$ pick a cut-off $\psi_n\in C^\infty([0,t])$ with $\psi_n(t)=1$,
	$\psi_n(\tau)=0$ for $\tau\le t-\frac1n$ and $0\le\psi_n\le1$, and set
	$x_n(\tau):=g_n(\tau)+\psi_n(\tau)a$. Then
	$x_n\in C^\infty([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d)\subset H^1([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $x_n(t)=a$, so that
	$|x_n(t)-a|=0$ for every $n$. As for the $L^2$-component, the triangle inequality gives
	$\|x_n-f\|_{L^2}\le\|g_n-f\|_{L^2}+\|\psi_na\|_{L^2}$, where the first term vanishes in
	the limit while
	\[
		\|\psi_na\|_{L^2}^2=|a|^2\int_{t-1/n}^t|\psi_n(\tau)|^2d\tau
		\le\frac{|a|^2}{n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0 .
	\]
	Therefore $\|\Phi(x_n)-(a,f)\|_{\mathcal K}\to0$, and since $\Phi$ is an isometry onto
	a dense subspace of the complete space $\mathcal K$, the claim follows.
head: environment

label: lem:boundedextension
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:boundedextension}
	The quadratic mapping $\widehat{H^t}$ is bounded on $\mathcal K$: there exists $K>0$,
	independent of $t\in(0,t_0]$, such that
	\[
		\left|\lambda(t)\widehat{H^t}(a,f)\right|
		\le K\left(|a|^2+\|f\|_{L^2([0,t],\mathbb{R}^{d-1})}^2\right).
	\]
	Consequently, \eqref{eq:hessGnoV1} extends uniquely to a continuous quadratic form on
	$\mathcal K$, which coincides with \eqref{eq:extensHessian}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
All the vector fields $X^\tau_j$, $\dot X^\tau_j$ and their brackets, evaluated at
	$q(t)$ and paired with $\lambda(t)$, are continuous functions of
	$(t,\tau)\in[0,t_0]^2$, hence the bilinear forms on $\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{R}^{d-1}$ defined by them have operator norms
	uniformly bounded by a constant $K_0>0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(iv). Estimating the three summands separately and using
	$\|f\|_{L^1}\le\sqrt t\,\|f\|_{L^2}\le\|f\|_{L^2}$, valid for $t\le1$, we obtain
	\[
		\left|\lambda(t)\widehat{H^t}(a,f)\right|
		\le K_0\|f\|_{L^2}^2+K_0|a|\,\|f\|_{L^1}+K_0\|f\|_{L^1}^2
		\le K\left(|a|^2+\|f\|_{L^2}^2\right)
	\]
	with $K:=\frac52K_0$, where we used
	$|a|\,\|f\|_{L^2}\le\frac12(|a|^2+\|f\|_{L^2}^2)$. The extension statement follows
	from Proposition~\ref{prop:completion} and the density of $H^1([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d)$ in
	$\mathcal K$.
head: environment

label: lem:conenorm
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Expanding the constraint gives $|v(\tau)|^2\le-2v_1(\tau)-v_1(\tau)^2$, whence
	\[
		\left|\mathbf v(\tau)\right|^2=v_1(\tau)^2+\left|v(\tau)\right|^2
		\le-2v_1(\tau)=2\left|v_1(\tau)\right| ,
	\]
	where we used \eqref{eq:cone}. Moreover $\big(1+v_1(\tau)\big)^2\le1$ forces
	$-2\le v_1(\tau)\le0$, which gives the second inequality in \eqref{eq:pointwisecone}
	and, in turn, $\|\mathbf v\|_{L^1}\le2t$. Integrating \eqref{eq:pointwisecone} over $[0,t]$
	and using $V_1(0)=0$ together with $v_1\le0$ we obtain
	\[
		\left\|\mathbf v\right\|_{L^2}^2\le2\int_0^t\left|v_1(\tau)\right|d\tau
		=-2\int_0^tv_1(\tau)\,d\tau=-2V_1(t)=2\left|V_1(t)\right| ,
	\]
	and $|V_1(t)|\le\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}$ by the very definition of
	$\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal H}$.
head: environment

label: rmk:nonhomog
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:nonhomog}
	Estimate \eqref{eq:conenorm} is the structural fact on which the whole remainder
	analysis rests: on the admissible set the square of the strong $L^2$-norm of the
	control is dominated by the first power of the weak norm of its primitive. The
	inequality is of course not homogeneous -- the admissible set is not a linear subspace -- and
	this is precisely what renders a cubic remainder quadratic in $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal H}$,
	with a small prefactor, rather than merely of order $3/2$. Geometrically, the admissible set
	forces a variation to ``pay'' in the direction $-e_1$, i.e.\ in length, for any
	transverse displacement it produces; \eqref{eq:conenorm} is the quantitative form of
	this trade-off.
head: environment

label: lem:localization
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Localization

title: Proof
body_md:
The right-hand side of \eqref{eq:perturbedode} is measurable in $\tau$, smooth in $x$ on
	$\mathcal B$ with derivatives bounded uniformly by Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(iv), and
	bounded by $L_0|\mathbf v(\tau)|$, so that a unique local solution exists. As long as the
	solution stays in the ball of radius $\delta$ centred at the origin, which is contained
	in the translated set $\mathcal B$ by Remark~\ref{rmk:chart}(a), Lemma~\ref{lem:conenorm}
	gives
	\[
		\left|q_{\mathbf v}(\tau)\right|
		\le\int_0^\tau\left|X^\theta_{\mathbf v(\theta)}\big(q_{\mathbf v}(\theta)\big)\right|d\theta
		\le L_0\|\mathbf v\|_{L^1([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d)}\le2L_0t<\delta ,
	\]
	where the last inequality is Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(v). Since the bound is strictly
	smaller than $\delta$, the solution cannot reach the boundary of that ball, and a
	standard continuation argument shows that it exists on the whole interval $[0,t]$.
head: environment

label: lem:defect
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x^1,\dots,x^n$ denote the coordinate functions of Remark~\ref{rmk:chart}(a),
	centred at $q(t)$. For a fixed $m\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, the Volterra expansion
	\eqref{eq:Volterra_expansion} with $N=1$ yields
	\[
		x^m\big(q_{\mathbf v}(t)\big)
		=\int_0^t\Big(0\circ X^{\tau_1}_{\mathbf v(\tau_1)}\Big)x^m\,d\tau_1
		+\int_{\Sigma_2(t)}\Big(q_{\mathbf v}(\tau_2)\circ X^{\tau_2}_{\mathbf v(\tau_2)}
		\circ X^{\tau_1}_{\mathbf v(\tau_1)}\Big)x^m\,d\tau_2d\tau_1 .
	\]
	Since the coordinate functions are linear, the first summand is precisely the $m$-th
	component of $d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)$, and the second one is therefore the $m$-th component
	of the defect $G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)-d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)$. To estimate it, set
	\[
		\Lambda_2:=\max_{m,i,j}\ \sup_{[0,t_0]^2\times\mathcal B}
		\left|\Big(X^{\tau_2}_jX^{\tau_1}_ix^m\Big)(x)\right| ,
	\]
	which is finite and independent of $t$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(iv); recall that
	$q_{\mathbf v}(\tau_2)\in\mathcal B$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:localization}. Enlarging the
	simplex $\Sigma_2(t)$ to the square $[0,t]^2$, which is legitimate because the
	integrand is bounded in modulus by a non-negative function, we get
	\[
		\left|\left(G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)-d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right)^m\right|
		\le\Lambda_2\,d^2\,\left\|\mathbf v\right\|_{L^1([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d)}^2 .
	\]
	By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and Lemma~\ref{lem:conenorm},
	$\|\mathbf v\|_{L^1}^2\le t\|\mathbf v\|_{L^2}^2\le2t\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}$, so that
	\eqref{eq:defectest} holds with $C_Q:=2\sqrt n\,\Lambda_2\,d^2$, after summing the $n$
	components.
head: environment

label: rmk:defectnonhomog
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:defectnonhomog}
	Estimate \eqref{eq:defectest} is, once more, non-homogeneous: the left-hand side -- the
	quadratic defect of the first differential -- is a genuinely quadratic quantity
	in $\mathbf v$, while the right-hand side is linear in $\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}$. This is not a
	weakness but the whole point. The defect will be compared, in
	Proposition~\ref{prop:perturbedKer}, with the boundary values $V_i(t)$, which are
	homogeneous of degree one in the variation; a homogeneous quadratic bound would be
	useless there for large variations, whereas the small prefactor $t$ makes the
	comparison effective uniformly on the whole admissible set. As in Remark~\ref{rmk:nonhomog}, the
	gain lies in the prefactor, not in the exponent.
head: environment

label: prop:perturbedKer
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:C0-perturbedker
title: Proof
body_md:
For $i=1,\dots,d$ define
	$C_i(t):=\int_0^t\sum_{j=2}^d\left|\left\langle\eta_i(t),\dot X_j^\tau(q(t))
	\right\rangle\right|^2d\tau$. The map
	$(t,\tau)\mapsto\left\langle\eta_i(t),\dot X_j^\tau(q(t))\right\rangle$ is continuous on
	the compact triangle $\{(t,\tau)\mid0\le\tau\le t\le t_0\}$: indeed $t\mapsto q(t)$ and
	$t\mapsto\eta_i(t)$ are continuous, while the transported fields and their time
	derivatives depend smoothly on the relevant variables by Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(iv).
	Therefore
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:C0-perturbedker}
		C_0:=\sup_{0\le t\le t_0}\max_{1\le i\le d}C_i(t)<\infty ,
	\end{equation}
	and $C_0$ depends only on the reference extremal, the adapted frame, the coframe and
	$t_0$, neither on $\mathbf v$ nor on $t$.

	Integrating by parts in \eqref{eq:fdif} with respect to $\tau$ we obtain
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:first-differential-boundary}
		\begin{aligned}
			d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)&=q(t)\circ\int_0^tX^\tau_{\mathbf v(\tau)}\,d\tau
			=q(t)\circ X^t_{\mathbf V(t)}-q(t)\circ\int_0^t\dot X^\tau_{\mathbf V(\tau)}\,d\tau\\
			&=V_1(t)X_1(q(t))+\sum_{j=2}^dV_j(t)X_j(q(t))
			-\int_0^t\dot X^\tau_{V(\tau)}(q(t))\,d\tau ,
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	where we used $\mathbf V(0)=0$, $X_i^t=X_i$ for every $i$, and \eqref{eq:X1_identity} to
	cancel $\dot X_1^\tau$ inside the integral. Fix $i\in\{1,\dots,d\}$; evaluating
	\eqref{eq:first-differential-boundary} against $\eta_i(t)$ and using \eqref{eq:coframe},
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Vi-perturbedker}
		V_i(t)=\int_0^t\sum_{j=2}^dV_j(\tau)
		\left\langle\eta_i(t),\dot X_j^\tau(q(t))\right\rangle d\tau
		+\left\langle\eta_i(t),d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right\rangle .
	\end{equation}
	The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and \eqref{eq:C0-perturbedker} bound the first summand
	by $\sqrt{C_0}\,\|V\|_{L^2([0,t],\mathbb{R}^{d-1})}$. As for the second one,
	Lemma~\ref{lem:defect} and the triangle inequality give
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:dG-bound-perturbedker}
		\left|d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right|\le\left|G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right|
		+C_Q\,t\,\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H} ,
	\end{equation}
	and $|\eta_i(t)|\le C_\eta$. Combining the two estimates yields
	\eqref{eq:perturbedkerest}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Proposition~\ref{prop:perturbedKer} is the point at which the end-point constraint enters the analysis in a quantitative way. Indeed, the strong Legendre condition yields coercivity only on the bulk quantity $\|V\|_{L^2}$, while the reduced Hessian depends on the stronger pair $(V(t),V)$ and therefore on the boundary value $V(t)$ as well. Estimate~\eqref{eq:perturbedkerest} recovers the boundary values $V_i(t)$ from the end-point defect $G_{q(t)}^t(\mathbf v)$, showing that the latter controls the missing component of the norm. In particular, for exact competitors satisfying $G_{q(t)}^t(\mathbf v)=0$, the boundary term $V(t)$ becomes comparable to $\|V\|_{L^2}$ for sufficiently small $t$. This observation is what ultimately allows the Legendre coercivity to be upgraded from $\|V\|_{L^2}$ to the full norm $\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:perturbednorm} and Theorem~\ref{thm:perturbedcoercivity}.

label: eq:squaredendpoint
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $N:=\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}$, $L:=\|V\|_{L^2([0,t],\mathbb{R}^{d-1})}$,
	$\theta:=C_\eta C_Q\,t$, $D:=\left|G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right|$ and $\beta:=C_\eta D$, so
	that \eqref{eq:perturbedkerest} reads $|V_i(t)|\le\sqrt{C_0}\,L+\theta N+\beta$ for
	$i=1,\dots,d$. Squaring and using $(x+y+z)^2\le3(x^2+y^2+z^2)$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:squaredendpoint}
		|V_i(t)|^2\le3\left(C_0L^2+\theta^2N^2+\beta^2\right),\qquad i=1,\dots,d .
	\end{equation}
	As in Lemma~\ref{lem:conenorm}, constraint \eqref{eq:cone} gives $\dot V_1\le0$ a.e.,
	so that $V_1$ is non-increasing with $V_1(0)=0$, whence $|V_1(\tau)|\le|V_1(t)|$ for
	every $\tau\in[0,t]$ and $\|V_1\|_{L^2([0,t])}^2\le t\,|V_1(t)|^2\le|V_1(t)|^2$, the
	last inequality because $t\le1$. Summing,
	\[
		N^2=\sum_{i=1}^d|V_i(t)|^2+\|V_1\|_{L^2}^2+L^2
		\le(d+1)\max_i|V_i(t)|^2+L^2 ,
	\]
	and by \eqref{eq:squaredendpoint}, with $A:=3(d+1)$,
	$N^2\le A\left(C_0L^2+\theta^2N^2+\beta^2\right)+L^2$. Choose $t_1\in(0,t_0]$ so small
	that $A\theta^2=AC_\eta^2C_Q^2t^2\le\frac12$ for every $t\in(0,t_1]$; absorbing
	$A\theta^2N^2$ into the left-hand side we obtain
	$N^2\le2\left(AC_0+1\right)L^2+2A\beta^2$, which is \eqref{eq:perturbednormequiv} with
	$C_1:=\sqrt{2(AC_0+1)}$ and $C_2:=C_\eta\sqrt{2A}$.

body_md:
\label{lem:transport}
	For every $\tau\in[0,t]$ and every $w\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}$,
	\[
		\left\langle\lambda(t),\left[\dot X^{\tau}_{w},X^{\tau}_{w}\right](q(t))
		\right\rangle
		=\left\langle\lambda(\tau),\left[\dot X_{w},X_{w}\right](q(\tau))\right\rangle
		=Q^{\tau}(w).

name: Transport of the Legendre form

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition $X^\tau=e^{(t-\tau)X_1}_*X$, and the pushforward by a diffeomorphism is
	an isomorphism of Lie algebras, so that
	$\left[\dot X^\tau_w,X^\tau_w\right]=e^{(t-\tau)X_1}_*\left[\dot X_w,X_w\right]$.
	Evaluating at $q(t)=e^{(t-\tau)X_1}(q(\tau))$ and recalling \eqref{eq:covectcurve},
	which gives $\lambda(\tau)=\big(e^{(t-\tau)X_1}\big)^*\lambda(t)$, the claim follows
	from the definition of pullback.

label: thm:perturbedcoercivity
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:coercivityinL
title: Proof
body_md:
We keep the notation $N,L,D,\theta,\beta$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:perturbednorm} and
	decompose, following \eqref{eq:hessGnoV1} and \eqref{eq:extensHessian},
	$\lambda(t)\widehat{H^t}\big(V(t),V\big)=I_1(V)+I_2\big(V(t),V\big)$, where
	\[
		\begin{aligned}
			I_1(V)&:=\int_0^t\left\langle\lambda(t),
			\left[\dot X^{\tau}_{V(\tau)},X^{\tau}_{V(\tau)}\right](q(t))
			\right\rangle d\tau,\\
			I_2\big(V(t),V\big)&:=\int_0^t\left\langle\lambda(t),
			\left[X_{V(t)}+\int_0^{\tau}\dot X^{\theta}_{V(\theta)}\,d\theta,\,
			\dot X^{\tau}_{V(\tau)}\right](q(t))\right\rangle d\tau .
		\end{aligned}
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:transport} and the strong Legendre condition \eqref{eq:slg1},
	\[
		I_1(V)=\int_0^tQ^{\tau}\big(V(\tau)\big)\,d\tau\ge c\,L^2 ,
	\]
	an estimate which involves no constraint on $\mathbf v$ whatsoever. As for $I_2$, let
	$K_0>0$ be a uniform bound, on $[0,t_0]^2$, for the operator norms of the bilinear forms
	$(a,b)\mapsto\langle\lambda(t),[X_a,\dot X^{\tau}_b](q(t))\rangle$ and
	$(a,b)\mapsto\langle\lambda(t),[\dot X^{\theta}_a,\dot X^{\tau}_b](q(t))\rangle$ on
	$\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{R}^{d-1}$, which exists by Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(iv) and may be taken
	equal to the constant of Lemma~\ref{lem:boundedextension}. Splitting $I_2$ into its two summands and
	using $\|V\|_{L^1}\le\sqrt tL$ we get
	\[
		\left|I_2\big(V(t),V\big)\right|\le K_0\,|V(t)|\,\sqrt t\,L+K_0\,t\,L^2 .
	\]
	By Propositions~\ref{prop:perturbedKer} and~\ref{prop:perturbednorm} we have both
	$|V(t)|\le\sqrt d\max_{i\ge2}|V_i(t)|$ and, for $t\le t_1$, $N\le C_1L+C_2D$.
	Therefore
	\[
		|V(t)|\le\sqrt d\left(\sqrt{C_0}\,L+\theta N+\beta\right)
		\le\sqrt d\left(\sqrt{C_0}+\theta C_1\right)L
		+\sqrt d\left(\theta C_2+C_\eta\right)D=:c_4L+c_5D,
	\]
	where $c_4,c_5$ are independent of $t\in(0,t_1]$ because
	$\theta=C_\eta C_Qt\le C_\eta C_Q$. Hence
	\[
		\left|I_2\right|\le\left(K_0c_4\sqrt t+K_0t\right)L^2+K_0c_5\sqrt t\,D\,L .
	\]
	Choose $t_2\in(0,t_1]$ so small that $K_0c_4\sqrt t+K_0t\le\frac c2$ for every
	$t\in(0,t_2]$; then
	$\lambda(t)\widehat{H^t}\big(V(t),V\big)\ge\frac c2L^2-K_0c_5\,D\,L$. By the Young
	inequality $K_0c_5DL\le\frac c4L^2+\frac{(K_0c_5)^2}{c}D^2$ we obtain
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:coercivityinL}
		\lambda(t)\widehat{H^t}\big(V(t),V\big)\ \ge\ \frac c4L^2
		-\frac{(K_0c_5)^2}{c}D^2 .
	\end{equation}
	Finally, Proposition~\ref{prop:perturbednorm} gives
	$L^2\ge\big(N^2-C_2^2D^2\big)/C_1^2$, so that
	\[
		\lambda(t)\widehat{H^t}\big(V(t),V\big)\ \ge\ \frac{c}{4C_1^2}N^2
		-\left(\frac{cC_2^2}{4C_1^2}+\frac{(K_0c_5)^2}{c}\right)D^2 ,
	\]
	which is \eqref{eq:perturbedcoercivity} with $\gamma_*:=\frac{c}{4C_1^2}$ and
	$C_3:=\frac{cC_2^2}{4C_1^2}+\frac{(K_0c_5)^2}{c}$.
head: environment

label: rmk:conjugate
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:conjugate}
	Estimate \eqref{eq:coercivityinL} is the heart of the matter, and it deserves a
	geometric reading. The term $I_1$ is, by Lemma~\ref{lem:transport}, the integral of the
	Legendre form along the extremal: it is the only term of the second variation carrying
	a sign, and it is positive definite by hypothesis. All the remaining terms are
	length-three brackets paired with $\lambda(t)$ whose contribution carries a factor
	$\sqrt t$ or $t$, coming from H\"older's inequality on an interval of length $t$. Short
	time therefore plays here the role that the absence of conjugate points plays in the
	classical Jacobi theory: it guarantees that the indefinite part of the second variation
	has not yet had the time to overcome the definite one. What the argument does
	not provide is the sharp threshold, i.e.\ the first conjugate time.

label: lem:cubicremainder
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Third-order expansion

label: eq:volterra-at
title: Proof
body_md:
With $L_0$ and $\delta$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(v) one has
	$\left|X^\tau_{\mathbf w}(x)\right|\le L_0|\mathbf w|$ for every $\mathbf w\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $x\in\mathcal B$,
	and by Lemma~\ref{lem:localization} the trajectory $q_{\mathbf v}$ stays in $\mathcal B$ for
	every $\tau\in[0,t]$. The Volterra expansion~\eqref{eq:Volterra_expansion}
	with $N=2$, applied to the function $a_t$ and evaluated at $q(t)=0$, yields
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:volterra-at}
		a_t\big(G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\big)
		=\int_0^t\Big(X_{\mathbf v(\tau_1)}^{\tau_1}a_t\Big)(q(t))\,d\tau_1
		+\int_{\Sigma_2(t)}\Big(X_{\mathbf v(\tau_2)}^{\tau_2}\circ X_{\mathbf v(\tau_1)}^{\tau_1}
		a_t\Big)(q(t))\,d\tau_2d\tau_1+R^t(\mathbf v),
	\end{equation}
	with $R^t(\mathbf v)$ as in \eqref{eq:remainderintegral}. Because $d_{q(t)}a_t=\lambda(t)$
	and $a_t$ is affine, the first term equals
	$\left\langle\lambda(t),d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right\rangle$, which vanishes by
	abnormality. The second term is $\frac12\big(d_0^2G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\big)a_t$, and by
	\eqref{eq:Second_order_differential} it splits into the bracket part and the
	second-order part:
	\[
		\frac12\int_{\Sigma_2(t)}\left\langle\lambda(t),
		\left[X^{\tau_2}_{\mathbf v(\tau_2)},X^{\tau_1}_{\mathbf v(\tau_1)}\right](q(t))\right\rangle
		d\tau_2d\tau_1
		+\frac12\left(q(t)\circ W_{\mathbf v}\circ W_{\mathbf v}\right)a_t .
	\]
	By \eqref{eq:cruc_vanishing}, \eqref{eq:hessGnoV1} and \eqref{eq:extensHessian}, the
	first summand is $\frac12\lambda(t)\widehat{H^t}\big(V(t),V\big)$, and the second one
	is $S^t(\mathbf v)$. This proves \eqref{eq:exactexpansion}.  Since $a_t$ is affine, for any smooth vector field
	$W$ on $\mathcal B$ one has $\left(W\circ W\right)a_t
	=\left\langle\ell_t,D_xW\cdot W\right\rangle$. Integrating by parts as in
	\eqref{eq:first-differential-boundary} and using \eqref{eq:X1_identity},
	\[
		W_{\mathbf v}=X^t_{\mathbf V(t)}-\int_0^t\dot X^\tau_{V(\tau)}\,d\tau ,
	\]
	so that, by Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(iv), there is $\Lambda_3>0$ with
	\[
		\sup_{x\in\mathcal B}\left\|D_xW_{\mathbf v}(x)\right\|
		\le\Lambda_3\left(|\mathbf V(t)|+\|V\|_{L^1}\right)
		\le2\Lambda_3\,\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H},
	\]
	where we used $\|V\|_{L^1}\le\sqrt t\|V\|_{L^2}\le\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}$. On the other
	hand $W_{\mathbf v}(q(t))=d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)$ by \eqref{eq:fdif}, whence by
	\eqref{eq:dG-bound-perturbedker}
	\[
		\left|S^t(\mathbf v)\right|\le\frac12\,C_\ell\left\|D_xW_{\mathbf v}\right\|
		\left|d_0G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right|
		\le C_S\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}\left(\left|G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right|
		+C_Q\,t\,\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}\right)
	\]
	with $C_S:=C_\ell\Lambda_3$. For $i,j,k\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define the
	coefficients
	\[
		c_{kji}^t(\tau_3,\tau_2,\tau_1;x):=\Big(x\circ X_k^{\tau_3}\circ X_j^{\tau_2}
		\circ X_i^{\tau_1}\Big)a_t .
	\]
	Since $a_t$ is affine, its coordinate derivatives of order at least two vanish; thus
	$c^t_{kji}$ involves only $\ell_t$, the coordinate expressions of the transported
	fields, and their spatial derivatives up to order two; consequently
	$\partial_{\tau_3}c^t_{kji}$ and $D_xc^t_{kji}$ involve derivatives of the transported
	fields with respect to $x$ and $\tau$ of total order at most three. By
	Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted}(iii)--(iv) there is $\Lambda>0$ with
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:cubic-coefficient-bound}
		\left|c_{kji}^t\right|+\left|\partial_{\tau_3}c_{kji}^t\right|
		+\left|D_xc_{kji}^t\right|\le\Lambda
	\end{equation}
	for every $t\in(0,t_2]$, $x\in\mathcal B$ and $0\le\tau_3\le\tau_2\le\tau_1\le t$.
	Expanding the three perturbation fields in \eqref{eq:remainderintegral},
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:remainder-components}
		R^t(\mathbf v)=\sum_{i,j,k=1}^d\int_{\Sigma_3(t)}
		v_k(\tau_3)v_j(\tau_2)v_i(\tau_1)\,
		c_{kji}^t\big(\tau_3,\tau_2,\tau_1;q_{\mathbf v}(\tau_3)\big)\,d\tau_3d\tau_2d\tau_1 .
	\end{equation}
	Estimating \eqref{eq:remainder-components} directly by $\|\mathbf v\|_{L^1}^3$ would only
	give a term of order $\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}^{3/2}$. We therefore integrate by parts in
	$\tau_3$, the innermost variable of the simplex $0\le\tau_3\le\tau_2\le\tau_1\le t$.
	For fixed $\tau_1,\tau_2,i,j,k$ put
	$h_{kji}(\tau):=c_{kji}^t\big(\tau,\tau_2,\tau_1;q_{\mathbf v}(\tau)\big)$; this map is
	absolutely continuous and, by \eqref{eq:perturbedode}, \eqref{eq:pointwisecone} and
	\eqref{eq:cubic-coefficient-bound},
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:hprime}
		\left|h_{kji}(\tau)\right|\le\Lambda,
		\qquad
		\left|h_{kji}'(\tau)\right|\le\left|\partial_{\tau_3}c^t_{kji}\right|
		+\left|D_xc^t_{kji}\right|\,\left|X^\tau_{\mathbf v(\tau)}(q_{\mathbf v}(\tau))\right|
		\le\Lambda\left(1+2L_0\right)=:\Lambda_1 ,
	\end{equation}
	uniformly in $\tau_1,\tau_2,\tau$ and in $t\in(0,t_2]$. Since $V_k(0)=0$,
	\[
		\int_0^{\tau_2}h_{kji}(\tau_3)v_k(\tau_3)\,d\tau_3
		=h_{kji}(\tau_2)V_k(\tau_2)-\int_0^{\tau_2}h_{kji}'(\tau_3)V_k(\tau_3)\,d\tau_3 ,
	\]
	so that $R^t(\mathbf v)=A^t(\mathbf v)+B^t(\mathbf v)$, where
	\[
		\begin{aligned}
			A^t(\mathbf v)&:=\sum_{i,j,k}\int_{\Sigma_2(t)}h_{kji}(\tau_2)\,V_k(\tau_2)\,
			v_j(\tau_2)\,v_i(\tau_1)\,d\tau_2d\tau_1,\\
			B^t(\mathbf v)&:=-\sum_{i,j,k}\int_{\Sigma_3(t)}h_{kji}'(\tau_3)\,V_k(\tau_3)\,
			v_j(\tau_2)\,v_i(\tau_1)\,d\tau_3d\tau_2d\tau_1 .
		\end{aligned}
	\]
	Enlarging the simplices to the corresponding cubes and using \eqref{eq:hprime},
	\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\left|A^t(\mathbf v)\right|&\le\Lambda d^3\int_0^t\!\!\int_0^{t}
			\left|\mathbf V(\tau_2)\right|\left|\mathbf v(\tau_2)\right|\left|\mathbf v(\tau_1)\right|
			d\tau_2d\tau_1\\
			&\le\Lambda d^3\,\|\mathbf V\|_{L^2}\|\mathbf v\|_{L^2}\|\mathbf v\|_{L^1}
			\le\Lambda d^3\sqrt t\,\|\mathbf V\|_{L^2}\|\mathbf v\|_{L^2}^2,\\
			\left|B^t(\mathbf v)\right|&\le\Lambda_1d^3\,\|\mathbf V\|_{L^1}\|\mathbf v\|_{L^1}^2
			\le\Lambda_1d^3\,t^{3/2}\|\mathbf V\|_{L^2}\|\mathbf v\|_{L^2}^2
			\le\Lambda_1d^3\sqrt t\,\|\mathbf V\|_{L^2}\|\mathbf v\|_{L^2}^2 ,
		\end{aligned}
	\]
	the last inequality because $t\le1$. Finally, Lemma~\ref{lem:conenorm} gives
	$\|\mathbf v\|_{L^2}^2\le2\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}$, while trivially
	$\|\mathbf V\|_{L^2}\le\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}$; therefore
	$\left|R^t(\mathbf v)\right|\le C_R\sqrt t\,\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}^2$ with
	$C_R:=2(\Lambda+\Lambda_1)d^3$, which is \eqref{eq:remainderestimate}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $N:=\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}$ and $D:=\left|G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right|$. By
	Lemma~\ref{lem:cubicremainder} and Theorem~\ref{thm:perturbedcoercivity},
	\[
		\left\langle\ell_t,G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right\rangle
		=\frac12\lambda(t)\widehat{H^t}\big(V(t),V\big)+S^t(\mathbf v)+R^t(\mathbf v)
		\ \ge\ \frac{\gamma_*}2N^2-\frac{C_3}2D^2
		-\left|S^t(\mathbf v)\right|-\left|R^t(\mathbf v)\right| .
	\]
	By \eqref{eq:remainderestimate},
	$\left|R^t(\mathbf v)\right|+\left|S^t(\mathbf v)\right|
	\le\left(C_R\sqrt t+C_SC_Qt\right)N^2+C_SND$, and by the Young inequality
	$C_SND\le\frac{\gamma_*}8N^2+\frac{2C_S^2}{\gamma_*}D^2$. Hence
	\[
		\left\langle\ell_t,G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\right\rangle
		\ \ge\ \left(\frac{3\gamma_*}8-C_R\sqrt t-C_SC_Qt\right)N^2
		-\left(\frac{C_3}2+\frac{2C_S^2}{\gamma_*}\right)D^2 .
	\]
	Choosing $t_*\in(0,t_2]$ so small that $C_R\sqrt t+C_SC_Qt\le\frac{\gamma_*}8$ for
	every $t\in(0,t_*]$, we obtain \eqref{eq:separation} with $\eta:=\frac{\gamma_*}4$ and
	$C_4:=\frac{C_3}2+\frac{2C_S^2}{\gamma_*}$. Inequality \eqref{eq:separationdist}
	follows from $\left\langle\ell_t,x\right\rangle\le|\ell_t|\,|x|\le C_\ell|x|$.

label: rmk:onlyGoh
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:onlyGoh}
	The asymmetry between $\lambda(t)$ and the remaining elements of
	$\Lambda_t=\left(\mathrm{Im} d_0G^t_{q(t)}\right)^\perp$ is not a matter of convenience: it is
	built into the hypotheses, as anticipated in Subsection~\ref{ssec:onedir}. The Goh
	condition asserts the existence of at least one abnormal lift annihilating all
	the brackets $[X_i,X_j]$; it does not assert that every element of $\Lambda_t$ does the
	same. For $\mu\in\Lambda_t$ not satisfying Goh, the reduced Hessian
	$\mu\widehat{H^t}$ is not even well defined by \eqref{eq:extensHessian}, since the
	elimination of $V_1$ rests on \eqref{eq:cruc_vanishing}. An exact competitor, on the
	other hand, satisfies $\langle\mu,G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)\rangle=0$ for every
	$\mu\in\Lambda_t$, in particular for $\lambda(t)$: a strictly positive lower bound for
	the $\lambda(t)$-component alone already produces the contradiction.

name: Why $\lambda(t)$ is the only available covector

label: cor:rigidity
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Rigidity

title: Proof
body_md:
The left-hand side of \eqref{eq:separation} vanishes and so does its last term, whence
	$\eta\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le0$ and therefore $\|\mathbf V\|_{\mathcal H}=0$. Since
	$\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal H}$ dominates the $L^2$-norm of $\mathbf V$, we get $\mathbf V\equiv0$ and
	thus $\mathbf v=\dot{\mathbf V}\equiv0$.

label: thm:minimality
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:minimality}
	Let $u\in L^2([0,1],\mathbb{R}^d)$ be an arclength parametrized strictly singular control, and
	assume that the Goh condition \eqref{eq:Goh_section} and the strong Legendre condition
	\eqref{eq:strongLeg} hold along the corresponding nonzero abnormal lift
	$t\mapsto\lambda(t)$, with constant $c>0$. Then there exists $t_*\in(0,1]$ such that,
	for every $t\in(0,t_*]$, the restriction $u|_{[0,t]}$ minimizes the length
	\eqref{eq:length} among all admissible curves joining $q$ to $q(t)$: if
	$\gamma_{\tilde u}$ is an admissible curve with $F^t_q(\tilde u)=q(t)$ and
	$\ell(\gamma_{\tilde u})\le\ell(\gamma_{u^t})=t$, then $\ell(\gamma_{\tilde u})=t$ and
	$\gamma_{\tilde u}=\gamma_u|_{[0,t]}\circ\varphi$ for a nondecreasing absolutely
	continuous surjection $\varphi$ of $[0,t]$, that is, $\gamma_{\tilde u}$ coincides with
	$\gamma_u|_{[0,t]}$ up to reparametrization. If, in addition, $\tilde u$ has constant
	speed, then $\tilde u=u$. In particular $u|_{[0,t]}$ is the unique length-minimizing
	control of constant speed joining $q$ to $q(t)$.
head: environment
name: Short-time length minimality up to reparametrization

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $t\in(0,t_*]$, with $t_*$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:separation}, possibly further
	reduced so that $\overline B(q,t)\subset\mathcal O_1$, and let $\gamma_{\tilde u}$ be a
	competitor as in the statement. Since $\ell(\gamma_{\tilde u})\le t$, every point of
	$\gamma_{\tilde u}$ has sub-Riemannian distance at most $t$ from $q$, so that
	$\gamma_{\tilde u}\subset\overline B(q,t)\subset\mathcal O_1\subset\mathcal O$. Hence
	$\gamma_{\tilde u}$ is represented in the adapted frame of Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted} by a
	control $\tilde u\in L^2([0,t],\mathbb{R}^d)$, with the same length because both frames are
	orthonormal, and the end-point map is well defined on it. As observed in
	Subsection~\ref{ssec:adapted}, $\mathsf{L}(\tilde u)>0$. Apply
	Lemma~\ref{lem:reparam} and let $\tilde u_\varphi$ be the control of the curve $\eta$
	there. By the lemma
	$\left|\tilde u_\varphi(\tau)\right|=\ell(\gamma_{\tilde u})/t\le1$ for a.e.\ $\tau$,
	and the reparametrized curve has the same end-point as $\gamma_{\tilde u}$, so that
	$F^t_q(\tilde u_\varphi)=q(t)$. Writing
	$\mathbf v:=\tilde u_\varphi-u=(v_1,v)$ in the splitting \eqref{eq:boldnotation} and
	recalling $u=(1,0)$, the pointwise bound above reads
	\[
		\big(1+v_1(\tau)\big)^2+|v(\tau)|^2=\left|\tilde u_\varphi(\tau)\right|^2\le1,
		\qquad\text{a.e. }\tau\in[0,t],
	\]
	which is exactly \eqref{eq:conepointwise}. Moreover $G^t_{q(t)}(\mathbf v)=0$ by
	\eqref{eq:SLCEndpoint}. Corollary~\ref{cor:rigidity} then gives $\mathbf v\equiv0$, i.e.\
	$\tilde u_\varphi=u$ almost everywhere on $[0,t]$. In particular
	$\left|\tilde u_\varphi\right|\equiv1$, whence $\ell(\gamma_{\tilde u})=t$, and
	$\gamma_{\tilde u}=\gamma_{\tilde u_\varphi}\circ\varphi
	=\gamma_u|_{[0,t]}\circ\varphi$ is a reparametrization of the reference arc. If
	$\tilde u$ has constant speed, then $\dot\varphi\equiv1$ and $\varphi$ is the identity,
	because $\varphi(0)=0$, so that $\tilde u=u$.
